about: Read-only map of why only the town state and Congress sit and why Congress passes no policy law (laws lead, map-world-governing workflow, Oct 29): four readers, a planner and a completeness critic. The plan with the critic corrections applied is world-governing-plan-2026-10-29.md; the corrections are applied there, not here.

findings.claim: (a) Every state's session calendar comes from one data table read by sessionYear(): data/research/laws/state-session-calendars.json, which has rows for all 56 places (50 states, US-DC, US-AS, US-GU, US-MP, US-PR, US-VI) for 2025, 2026 and 2027: 168 rows, 107 SOURCED and 61 ESTIMATED. A year past the table repeats the latest year with the same odd/even parity, marked ESTIMATED. windowsIn() uses this table for states and congress-sessions.json for Congress.

(a) The game starts 2025-01-20, and all 56 places have a 2025 session row, so in a played year every legislature has a window. Sessions already sitting at the opening are picked up the next day (scheduleOpening with includeSitting). In 2026, MT, NV, ND and TX do not meet, and 11 places sit the full year.

(a) The other per-state rows a state act needs also cover all 56 places: effective-date rules, enacting clauses, and starting answers for all 54 platform questions. answerIn() works for any state key.
Only Congress and the town's own state are scheduled to open a session. Other states never get a session-open calendar entry, so they never sit.

(b) At the opening the offices engine seats only the town's state: stateOffices(stateKey, geoid) builds every chamber and every seat, each with a named official (personId null). openOfficials then turns every serving term with no person into a full person in one seatAll batch (fillInIdentity, tier 'calendar').

(b) Other states' chambers do NOT exist as offices at the opening. The officials engine seats only a sample: 8 members per chamber (stateSample.perChamber, TUNABLE), each standing for n/8 members (standsFor). Their seat ids are seat:<state>:<chamber>:sample:<party>:<i>, with no term and no office row.

(b) Because chamber() looks up offices by jurisdiction, it returns null for any state that has not been loaded. openSession then has no lower chamber and files nothing, and sessionChambers() and originChamber() are empty.

(b) The same builder already exists: officesOfState(api, stateKey). It builds a state's federal and state offices with every seat, a named official (seatNamedOfficial) and past terms, and runs only the first time anything reads that state. Today only the bench Politics screen and tests call it. The earlier pool item gov-other-state-legislatures closed on this on-demand design and left open whether seating every state up front is worth its cost.

(b) members() calls holderOf() on every seat. holderOf makes each named official a full person on first read through seatOfficial(), so any session that reads another state's chamber fills in all its members. seatOfficial runs colleagues(), which scans every officials row and every Congress delegation pair, once per call. Seating about 7,400 members one at a time during play would be quadratic; seating them in the opening batch costs one colleagues() pass.

(b) The roster's seatParties seats 7,420 members across 52 places (50 states, DC, PR). GU, VI, AS and MP have no roster; stateOffices seats them at large with party null under SG-GOV-territory-legislature-districts.

(c) Critical mis-file: billJurisdiction() returns the town's own state (lawChain(api).stateKey) for ANY state bill, and the town's own place for any city bill. Another state's act would be enacted as law:<town's state>:state:<question>:... and lawInForce would treat it as the town's state law, because levelRow matches on jurisdiction and level.
(c) effectiveRule() dates every state act by the town's state's effective-date rule.
(c) mootAtFloor() checks another state's bill against the town's state law, because it goes through billJurisdiction.

(c) The power checks read the TOWN's jurisdiction kind (federal-district or territory) for every body. In a DC or territory world, other states' bills are checked against the DC or territory column; in a state world, a territory's legislature is checked against the state column.

(c) filerOf() sets home = townLean(api) for every filer who is a full person. Every official is a full person, so every state legislator and member of Congress files weighted by the player's town's lean rather than their district's (districtLean is on the official row).
(c) The floor leader's order in every legislature is weighted by the town's residents' concern share.

(c, d) Settledness and reversal reluctance read across all jurisdictions: lastEnactment() uses the bySeriesOnly index. One state's fresh act would make the question 'fresh' for every body, including the town's own state, Congress and the council, and set their reversal reluctance from that act's margin.
(c) A few signing paths read the town's state for any body: the mayor veto rule, the line-item veto and the governor's veto window. They matter only on the player's desk.

(c) For other towns' bodies, two more paths read the town's own chain: countyOfBody uses the town's county, and recalls' weighOrdinance lets the town's adults weigh recalls over any city or county law.

(c) The interest-groups beforeVote hook runs on every bill. organizeResidents scans every town adult (viewOn), and employerStakes covers the town's employers, so town residents would organize over another state's bill. This is a mis-read and also a cost that scales with the number of bills.

(c) chamberVote emits office.voted for every member who is a full person (all officials), with no town filter; record.ts already filters vote-recorded to town news. Each chamber vote also emits legislative-vote with placeId set to the town.

(c) If officesOfState runs after openOfficials (the lazy path), the other state's governor seat seat:US-XX:governor gets a new term. holderOf then seats official:<termId>, and seatOfficial ends the opening governor (official:seat:US-XX:governor): a governor swap on first read. The Politics screen path can already trigger this today.

(c) Loading other states' federal offices, which officesOfState also does, would duplicate their House races. racesIn adds a seatRace for every us-house or legislature seat not covering the town in ANY state, and its roster loop adds every other state's House seats again. racesIn and nextRaceYear also scan every legislative seat in the offices table, not only the town's state that their comments describe.
(c) specs() passes townState into unrecordedParty for every held term. For seats with no roster party (the GU, VI, AS and MP at-large seats), the party fallback would read the town's state.

(c) If the sample members stay once real members are seated, bodyRead would count each chamber twice: it sums the officialsIn(body) party and wing means weighted by standsFor. The Nebraska sample also sits in body 'US-NE:legislature-legislature' while its office kind is legislature-unicameral.

(d) A law enacted in play is stored as law:<jurisdiction>:<level>:<series>:general:<effectiveDate>:<bill number>. With billJurisdiction fixed, another state's act would be law:US-NV:state:us-policy-positions:<question>:general:<date>:<number>. Today the laws table holds only the town's chain rows (openLaws loads startingLawRows(chain)), so the readers that span all jurisdictions are harmless until other states enact.

(d) Reads that would wrongly treat another state's correctly keyed law as the town's: (1) outcome-web lawValue returns 1 when ANY jurisdiction's latest row says yes (it reads bySeriesOnly); (2) lastEnactment and settledness, above; (3) lawTookEffect: when the row's jurisdiction is not in the town's chain, 'governing' is undefined, so it still emits law-took-effect with placeId=town and news=true, and computes before, ends and replacesLawId from the town's chain, so another state's repeal would read as the town's law ending; (4) law-reach runHandlers then reruns the town's handlers with the other state's lawId whenever the town's chain already has the law in force.

(d) Reads already safe against other states: lawInForce and levelRow filter to the chain's jurisdictions; localAuthority filters to chain.stateKey; policyAuthority's stateLaw reads only chain.stateKey; inForceForTown walks chain.levels; the withholding read (budgets.ts) resolves through the chain; the food-aid read filters to the governing row's jurisdiction.

How speed:year is measured: package.json runs scripts/speed-years/run.ts. It builds buildBenchWorld two-level with bookkeeping off and the place drawn from all 56 by the seed, times advanceCore over each 365-day year, and fails a year that is more than 1.2x the --baseline receipt (main on the same machine). The last recorded main base is about 120-130 s for Long Hill, seed m7b, so the 20 percent limit leaves roughly 24-26 s for all 55 extra legislatures (about 0.45 s each per year).

Cost per sitting day (estimated from the code; nothing was measured). M is the member count of both chambers: the roster averages 7,420/52 ≈ 143, New Hampshire about 424, Nebraska 49. A session-open day costs filerOf × M, plus up to 54 questions × M filingReason calls (about 7,700 at M=143), plus a positionOn per lower-chamber member for each question no member files. A floor-week day (one calendar day a week) takes up to perWeek = round(4 × 6) = 24 bills filed at least 21 days earlier. Each bill costs about M positionOn, the committee's positionOn, M legislature vote rows, M record-vote rows, M office.voted events, 1-2 legislative-vote events, an executive positionOn, and the before-vote hooks, including the interest-groups scan of town adults. A full floor day is therefore about 3,400 positionOn and about 10,000 row writes and events for an average state. Bills per session are capped by the 54 questions, and the existing pool item measured 10-19 changed questions per sitting. Empty floor weeks still run chamberBills, a full scan of the unindexed bills table.

findings.claim: A built world knows other towns only as reference data, never as records. Every locality in all 56 jurisdictions is in the place index (32,350 Census Gazetteer rows plus territory villages), keyed by GEOID.

Every general-purpose government is listed with its county area and the place it governs: 38,704 units, 19,489 municipalities, all with a county GEOID, and governmentUnitsForState(usps) returns a state's units. This is the data rule for finding other towns in the same county or state. 1,643 county areas hold 5 or more municipalities (median 5, largest 121), 378 hold exactly 1, and 77 county governments have none.

Each other town's population can already be read: placeReferencePopulation(geoid, seed) gives the world's figure (Census Vintage 2025, else ACS 2020-24, else the 2020 island-area count), with the same per-world spread the drawn town gets. County populations are in public-budget-bases countyPopulation2024.

No counted population and no people exist for other towns. Opening kin live in the county record or the state placeholder, 'never in the town itself'. Officials outside the town are calendar-tier people placed at a state key.

Only the drawn town's local offices are created. openOffices seats federal and own-state offices, then localOfficesForPlace(placeKey) for the town alone, all with coversTown true. The one lazy loader for 'elsewhere' is officesOfState, which covers another state's offices with coversTown false and named officials. No loader exists for another place's council or mayor.

Office data can already be built for any municipality. cityOffices builds a council (seat count read where known, else the ICMA modal size) and a mayor from data, with ids office:<gus id>:council and office:<gus id>:mayor and jurisdiction set to the gus unit id. localOfficesForPlace also returns the county board and county row offices, whose ids would match the drawn town's own county offices when the other town is in the same county.

The members of another town's council would become officials (thin saved people) automatically. members() calls holderOf, which calls seatOfficial and seats each serving term as an official the first time it is read. holderOf takes the state from the drawn town's stateKey for any non-state office, which is correct only for towns in the same state.
townBodies picks every office of kind council, county-board or township-board without filtering on coversTown. openWorldLegislating calls it once, at opening, with only the town's offices loaded.

scheduleMeeting and nextMeeting are already per office and act only on meeting days (a calendar entry local-meeting:<office>:<date>), with no daily scan. The interval comes from the body's size band. bodyPopulation reads the drawn town's referencePopulation for any council, so another town's council would meet on the drawn town's band.

localMeeting works out which government the body makes law for from the drawn town's chain, not from the body. A council always maps to chain.levels[last], the drawn town's place:<geoid>. needsChange reads inForceForTown (the drawn town's chain). allowed reads levelMayDecide, which reads the drawn town's state.

Agenda and filing read the drawn town's conditions: filerOf sets home = townLean(api) for any member who is a person (officials are), and the floor order weighs townConcernShare, which counts the drawn town's residents only.
Each other town's lean is available from data, the same way the town's own is set: districtLean(townDistrict(geoid, usps, 'congressional', date)).

LEAK: a council's law would be written as the drawn town's law. billJurisdiction returns chain.levels[last] (the drawn town) for every city-level body and chain.stateKey for every state body. effectiveRule and enact write the row under that jurisdiction. countyOfBody looks the county board up among governmentUnitsForPlace(drawn town), which only holds municipalities, so it always falls back to chain.countyGeoids[0].

Law rows are keyed by jurisdiction (id law:<jurisdiction>:<level>:<series>:general:<date>:<measure>; index bySeries = [jurisdiction, series]). Readers that go through the chain are safe from other places' rows: lawInForce/resolveLawInForce (levels from chain.levels, pending filtered to chain), yesLevels, answerIn, questionSettled, law-reach's inForce (via yesLevels), policyAuthority's stateLaw, the SNAP allotments read and budgets' residentLaw.

LEAK: readers that look a law up by series alone, in every jurisdiction: lastEnactment (the bySeriesOnly index), and through it settledness, lawStanding's reversal reluctance, the executive's lean and recordConsistency. Another town's fresh act would make the drawn town's law look fresh.

LEAK: outcome-web lawValue reads every jurisdiction's rows by series (index bySeriesOnly) and returns 1 when any jurisdiction's latest row is yes. Another town's or another state's enacted yes would move the drawn town's outcomes.

LEAK: lawTookEffect emits law-took-effect with placeId set to the drawn town and news:true for every row. Its governing check returns early only when the row's jurisdiction is a chain level, so an outside row still emits. The consumers are outcome-web (records the law and reruns), law-reach host, budgets, recalls, press and news ('*'), bench/changes.ts and bench/reached.ts.

Smaller leaks from the drawn town into other towns' bills. The town's interest groups lobby every council's members. draftBill's recordHomeRule targets the drawn town. mayorVeto reads the drawn town's population. budgetChambers and executivePriorities each take the first council or first city-level mayor found among all offices, so the answer depends on insertion order.

Coarser-level rule (DECISION-REGISTER Sept 26). Every other city and county meets on its real schedule, usually twice a month. On a meeting date that meeting is resolved: the agenda comes from that place's conditions and each member votes from their own saved record. Nothing is computed between meetings. Their laws are real records with real effects. Council members are real saved people, thin at first. So other towns may skip daily simulation, counted people, treasuries and individual residents. They may not skip their own law records or their own conditions driving the agenda.
